texts.2.9: 30.... Abide in me, and I in you
texts.2.18: 53.... Lines on the Death of Mrs. Stuart
texts.2.19: 57.... Summer Studies HOURS OF THE NIGHT.
texts.2.26: 88.... VII. When I awake I am still with Thee PRESSED FLOWERS FROM ITALY.
texts.2.27: 93.... A Day in the Pamfili Doria
texts.2.32: SLOW through the solemn air, in silence sailing,
texts.2.33: Borne by mysterious angels, strong and fair,
texts.2.34: She sleeps at last, blest dreams her eyelids veiling,
texts.2.35: Above this weary world of strife and care.
texts.2.36: Lo how she passeth!--dreamy, slow, and calm:
texts.2.37: Scarce wave those broad, white wings, so silvery bright;
texts.2.38: Those cloudy robes, in star-emblazoned folding,
texts.2.39: Sweep mistily athwart the evening light.
texts.2.40: Far, far below, the dim, forsaken earth,
texts.2.41: The foes that threaten, or the friends that weep;
texts.2.42: Past, like a dream, the torture and the pain:
texts.2.43: For so He giveth his beloved sleep.
texts.2.44: The restless bosom of the surging ocean
texts.2.45: Gives back the image as the cloud floats o'er,
texts.2.46: Hushing in glassy awe his troubled motion;
texts.2.47: For one blest moment he complains no more.
texts.2.48: Like the transparent golden floor of heaven,
texts.2.49: His charmed waters lie as in a dream,
texts.2.50: And glistening wings, and starry robes unfolding,
texts.2.51: And serious angel eyes far downward gleam.
texts.2.52: O restless sea! thou seemest all enchanted
texts.2.53: By that sweet vision of celestial rest;
texts.2.54: Where are the winds and tides thy peace that haunted,--
texts.2.55: So still thou seemest, so glorified and blest!
texts.2.56: Ah, sea! to-morrow, that sweet scene forgotten,
texts.2.57: Dark tides and tempests shall thy bosom rear;
texts.2.58: And thy complaining waves, with restless motion,
texts.2.59: Shall toss their hands in their old wild despair.
texts.2.60: So o'er our hearts sometimes the sweet, sad story
texts.2.61: Of suffering saints, borne homeward crowned and blest,
texts.2.62: Shines down in stillness with a tender glory,
texts.2.63: And makes a mirror there of breathless rest.
texts.2.64: For not alone in those old Eastern regions
texts.2.65: Are Christ's beloved ones tried by cross and chain;
texts.2.66: In many a house are his elect ones hidden,
texts.2.67: His martyrs suffering in their patient pain.
texts.2.68: The rack, the cross, life's weary wrench of woe,
texts.2.69: The world sees not, as slow, from day to day.
texts.2.70: In calm, unspoken patience, sadly still,
texts.2.71: The loving spirit bleeds itself away.
texts.2.72: But there are hours when, from the heavens unfolding,
texts.2.73: Come down the angels with the glad release;
texts.2.74: And we look upward, to behold in glory
texts.2.75: Our suffering loved ones borne away to peace.
texts.2.76: Ah, brief the calm! the restless wave of feeling
texts.2.77: Rises again when the bright cloud sweeps by,
texts.2.78: And our unrestful souls reflect no longer
texts.2.79: That tender vision of the upper sky.
texts.2.80: Espoused Lord of the pure saints in glory,
texts.2.81: To whom all faithful souls affianced are,
texts.2.82: Breathe down thy peace into our restless spirits,
texts.2.83: And make a lasting, heavenly vision there.
texts.2.84: So the bright gates no more on us shall close;
texts.2.85: No more the cloud of angels fade away;
texts.2.86: And we shall walk, amid life's weary strife,
texts.2.87: In the calm light of thine eternal day.
texts.2.88: According to this legend, Catherine was a noble maiden of Alexandria, distinguished alike by birth, riches, beauty, and the rarest gifts of genius and learning. In the flower of her life she consecrated herself to the service of her Redeemer, and cheerfully suffered for his sake the loss of wealth, friends, and the esteem of the world. Banishment, imprisonment, and torture were in vain tried to shake the constancy of her faith; and at last she was bound upon the torturing-wheel for a cruel death. But the angels descended, so says the story, rent the wheel, and bore her away, through the air, far over the sea, to Mount Sinai, where her body was left to repose, and her soul ascended with them to heaven.
texts.3.1: "Socrates. However, you and Simmias appear to me as if you wished to sift this subject more thoroughly, and to be afraid, like children, lest, on the soul's departure from the body, winds should blow it away.
texts.3.2: "Upon this Cebes said, 'Endeavor to teach us better, Socrates. Perhaps there is a childish spirit in our breast that has such a dread. Let us endeavor to persuade him not to be afraid of death, as of hobgoblins.'
texts.3.3: " 'But you must charm him every day,' said Socrates, 'until you have quieted his fears.'
texts.3.4: " 'But whence, O Socrates,' he said, 'can we procure a skilful charmer for such a case, now you are about to leave us.'
texts.3.5: "'Greece is wide, Cebes,' he said, 'and in it surely there are skilful men; and there are many barbarous nations, all of which you should search, seeking such a charmer, sparing neither money nor toil.' " -- Last words of Socrates, as narrated by Plato in the Phado.
texts.3.6: WE need that charmer, for our hearts are sore
texts.3.7: With longings for the things that may not be,
texts.3.8: Faint for the friends that shall return no more,

texts.23.87: And shall stand and feed as a shepherd
texts.23.88: The flock which his mercy calls,--
texts.23.89: O, then to those noble churches,
texts.23.90: To picture and statue and gem,
texts.23.91: To the pageant of solemn worship,
texts.23.92: Shall the meaning come back again.
texts.23.93: And this strange and ancient city,
texts.23.94: In that reign of His truth and love,
texts.23.95: Shall be what it seems in the twilight,
texts.23.96: The type of that City above.
texts.24.1: SWEET fountains, plashing with a dreamy fall,
texts.24.2: And mosses green, and tremulous veils of fern,
texts.24.3: And banks of blowing cyclamen, and stars,
texts.24.4: Blue as the skies, of myrtle blossoming,
texts.24.5: The twilight shade of ilex overhead
texts.24.6: O'erbubbling with sweet song of nightingale,
texts.24.7: With walks of strange, weird stillness, leading on
texts.24.8: 'Mid sculptured fragments half to green moss gone,
texts.24.9: Or breaking forth amid the violet leaves
texts.24.10: With some white gleam of an old world gone by.
texts.24.11: Ah! strange, sweet quiet! wilderness of calm,
texts.24.12: Gardens of dreamy rest, I long to lay
texts.24.13: Beneath your shade the last long sigh, and say,
texts.24.14: Here is my home, my Lord, thy home and mine;
texts.24.15: And I, having searched the world with many a tear,
texts.24.16: At last have found thee and will stray no more.
texts.24.17: But vainly here I seek the Gardener
texts.24.18: That Mary saw. These lovely halls beyond,
texts.24.19: That airy, sky-like dome, that lofty fane,
texts.24.20: Is as a palace whence the king is gone
texts.24.21: And taken all the sweetness with himself.
texts.24.22: Turn again, Jesus, and possess thine own!
texts.24.23: Come to thy temple once more as of old!
texts.24.24: Drive forth the money-changers, let it be
texts.24.25: A house of prayer for nations. Even so,
texts.25.1: O FAIREST mansion of a Father's love,
texts.25.3: Outspread to all, thy fountains ever full,
texts.25.4: And, fair as heaven, thy misty, sky-like dome
texts.25.5: Hung like the firmament with circling sweep
texts.25.7: That burn forever round the holy tomb.
texts.25.8: Most meet art thou to be the Father's house,
texts.25.9: The house of prayer for nations. Come the time
texts.25.10: When thou shalt be so! when a liberty,
texts.25.11: Wide as thine arms, high as thy lofty dome,
texts.25.12: Shall be proclaimed, by thy loud singing choirs,
texts.25.13: Like voice of many waters! Then the Lord
texts.25.14: Shall come into his temple, and make pure
texts.25.15: The sons of Levi; then, as once of old,
texts.25.16: The blind shall see, the lame leap as an hart,
texts.25.17: And to the poor the Gospel shall be preached,
texts.25.19: "The Lord is risen indeed," to die no more.
texts.25.20: Hasten it in its time. Amen! Amen!
texts.26.1: NOT of the earth that music! all things fade;
texts.26.2: Vanish the pictured walls! and, one by one,
texts.26.4: And now, O Jesus! round that silent cross
texts.26.5: A moment's pause, a hush as of the grave.
texts.26.6: Now rises slow a silver mist of sound,
texts.26.7: And all the heavens break out in drops of grief;
texts.26.8: A rain of sobbing sweetness, swelling, dying,
texts.26.9: Voice into voice inweaving with sweet throbs,
texts.26.10: And fluttering pulses of impassioned moan,--
texts.26.11: Veiled voices, in whose wailing there is awe.
texts.26.12: And mysteries of love and agony,
texts.26.13: A yearning anguish of celestial souls,
texts.26.14: A shiver as of wings trembling the air,
texts.26.15: As if God's shining doves, his spotless birds,
texts.26.16: Wailed with a nightingale's heart-break of grief,
texts.26.17: In this their starless night, when for our sins
texts.26.18: Their sun, their life, their love, hangs darkly there,
texts.26.19: Like a slain lamb, bleeding his life away!
